title: The hypertrophy series: maximum recoverable volume
summary: NH defines maximum recoverable volume (MRV) as the most volume you can recover and improve from. He argues an extra set within a session rarely hurts; the real risk is hitting the same muscle again too soon, so he gives each muscle two days. MRV is individual, found by experimentation, and should rise over time, driving ever-increasing tonnage. Most people undertrain from fear of overtraining, and strength gains without more tonnage won't build size.

claims.claim: He now expects the hypertrophy series to run about 20 parts rather than 10.
Maximum recoverable volume is the most volume your body can take without breaking, recover from and get better from; beyond it, work is wasted or causes regression.

Within a single session, one extra set (e.g. of squats) won't damage your progress unless you injure yourself doing it; at worst it adds no stimulus, and he believes more work always gives better results.
Superfluous volume matters more across the week: training the same body part again too soon is the real problem. If you kill your quads Monday, don't train them Tuesday.
Muscle protein synthesis lasts around 48 hours, so he always gives a muscle group two days to recover and never trains the same muscle two days in a row in his body-part split.
Light, non-strenuous work for a muscle trained the day before, just to bring in blood, can help recovery.
MRV differs between individuals; he does a lot of volume per session, which works for him but may not for you, so you must find your own through experimentation.
To optimise training you want to sit right at the brink of overtraining so you do all the work you can.

The vast majority of people undertrain; fear of overtraining makes them stop when tired, though the extra work done while tired is what drives results. That's why people train five years without the results they want.
Your MRV should keep climbing with age and training experience.
Always strive for more tonnage: if your bench tonnage is, say, 2000 at age 22, it should be much higher two years later, whether via more weight, reps or sets.
Getting stronger alone doesn't make you bigger: going from a 300 to a 400 lb squat while keeping tonnage the same won't add much leg size.
He thinks strength also plateaus without more tonnage for most people, because bigger muscles give the nervous system better leverage to move weight.
